slides.title: Everything you do is an operation.
slides.text: Reading a list, ticking an item, searching your notes, syncing with a friend: each is an operation, a small piece of JSON that says what to do. One engine runs them all.
slides.deep: An operation is JSON: {operation, data, …arguments}. One engine parses it, checks the rule, runs it locally and returns a result or a set of CRDT ops.

slides.title: A simple query.
slides.text: “What's still open, soonest first?” An operation takes data, narrows it and hands back an answer. It runs on your own device, over what you can already read.
slides.deep: find evaluates over the local decrypted state: filter (where), sort (order) and limit. Indexes are local and rebuilt from data the device can read.

slides.title: Changes are operations too.
slides.text: Ticking an item is an operation. The engine checks your rule, turns it into CRDT ops, signs them and hands them to sync. An operation is what you mean; CRDT ops are what gets stored.
slides.deep: update becomes one or more CRDT ops on the Doc, grouped into a change, signed by the signer, sealed into a chunk and announced.

slides.title: Walking a graph.
slides.text: Data links to data: a list to its items, an item to a photo, a person to their friends. A {walk} follows links hop by hop, and stops wherever your rules stop.
slides.deep: walk follows link fields across Docs to a given depth. Each hop needs read on the next piece of data; without it, the walk stops there.

slides.title: Searching by words.
slides.text: A {search} finds the notes that best match your words, ranked the way search engines do it (BM25). The index is built on your device, from what you can read, and never leaves it.
slides.deep: BM25 full-text ranking over a local inverted index built from readable data. Neither the index nor the query leaves the device.

slides.title: Searching by meaning.
slides.text: “Plumbing problems” should also find “water under the sink”. A {near} compares meaning as vectors and returns the closest entries. Same rule: the index is local.
slides.deep: near: vector similarity (for example cosine) over local embeddings, with an approximate nearest-neighbour index on the device. Embeddings are computed locally.

slides.title: Operations chain together.
slides.text: The answer of one operation is the input of the next. Search by meaning, follow the links to whoever is assigned, keep only what's open.
slides.deep: chain pipes the result set of each step into the next; each step is checked against its own required rule.

slides.title: New kinds of operations plug in.
slides.text: find, walk, search and near are {plugins}. Each one declares its name, the shape of its JSON, and what a rule must allow for it to run. A new plugin, say for maps or for time series, slots in the same way.
slides.deep: One plugin registry for operations (find, walk, near, act …) and for rule conditions (threshold, weights, time lock, at, where, limit …). Each plugin is named by the hash of its specification, declares its JSON shape, what a rule must allow, and, for conditions, whether it applies to identities or to data. Unknown plugins fail closed.

slides.title: Rules name the operations.
slides.text: Reading operations, like find, walk, search and near, need read on the data, and that's all: once your device can read it, the engine may search it any way you like. Change operations are where rules get fine: every device checks every signed change against them, down to one path or one matching entry.
slides.deep: Reading operations need read on the data and nothing else, because a reader holds the plaintext. Change operations are checked by every peer, down to a path or matching entry.

slides.title: Peers sync. They never ask.
slides.text: An operation runs only on your own device, over data you can read. No peer ever asks another peer a question about its data. Peers only carry what their rules allow, sealed. There's no client and no server, only peers. An always-on machine is just one more peer.
slides.deep: There is no query protocol between peers, only chunk sync. That removes trust in a remote answerer and inference attacks by repeated questions.

slides.title: Sharing an answer is sharing data.
slides.text: The street wants to know how many tasks are open in your home. It can't ask. Instead, your device counts and writes the number into a small piece of data of its own, with a rule that lets the street read it. The street sees the number and nothing else.
slides.deep: The answer is written as new data, computed and signed by your own device, with its own rule for the asker. That rule is revocable and expires like any other.

slides.title: The engine, in short.
list: Every read, change, search and sync is a JSON operation.
A change you do becomes CRDT ops that are signed and synced.
Operations chain: one answer feeds the next.
Operations run only on your device, over what you can read. Peers sync; they never ask.
Reading is allowed per piece of data; changes as finely as you like.
slides.deep: JSON operations, local execution, plugins, rules per operation, and peer-to-peer only. Your data, your device, your answers.
